**Short answer:** You can't safely stop paying rent yet, but you may be able to end your lease. Your lease promises working central air conditioning, so the landlord's failure to fix it can support ending the lease. To do that, you must first give the landlord a written notice that says you will end the lease over the AC. The portal request didn't say that, and the portal isn't a delivery method the statute names. If you leave without that notice, you risk owing rent for the rest of the lease. Holding back rent is weaker for you, because the AC is a lease promise and the statute's rent-withholding defense reaches only the repairs listed in section 83.51(1). Your rent for June is already paid, and July rent isn't due until July 1.

Have you handed or mailed the office anything in writing besides the portal request?

DETAILS

### Does the landlord have to fix the AC?
- Yes, under your lease. Section 11 says the landlord "will keep them in working order" and lists "central air conditioning" among the items.
- The statute's own repair list, section 83.51(1), doesn't name air conditioning. It covers building, housing, and health codes, plus structure and plumbing.
- A local housing code might cover AC, but the tool doesn't hold local codes. The Gainesville or Alachua County code office can tell you.
- You told me you don't know of any cause. Nothing suggests you or a guest broke it, so section 83.51(4) doesn't shift the blame to you.

### Can you end the lease?
Section 83.56(1) lets a tenant end the lease if the landlord "materially fails to comply with s. 83.51 (1) or material provisions of the rental agreement within 7 days after delivery of written notice by the tenant specifying the noncompliance and indicating the intention of the tenant to terminate the rental agreement." Here is where each condition stands:
1. **A duty the landlord failed:** Met in part. The AC is a lease promise (lease §11).
   - Whether the failure is "material" isn't settled, because the statute doesn't define the word.
   - One reading is that any failure of a lease promise counts.
   - The other reading looks at how serious it is, how long it has lasted, and how it affects living there. You told me it has been out since June 3 and it's about 90 degrees inside, which fits that second reading.
2. **A written notice, delivered a way the statute names, saying you will end the lease:** Not met.
   - Your June 4 portal request asked for a repair. It did not say you would end the lease, so it isn't this notice.
   - Section 83.56(4) names mailing, delivering a true copy, or e-mail under section 83.505. A portal message is not on that list.
   - Your lease has no e-mail addendum. Section 8 says you "have not agreed to deliver notices by e-mail."
   - Lease §7 says to hand-deliver notices to Suite A at 1840 SW 13th Street or send them there by certified mail. Doing either meets both the lease and the statute.
3. **Seven days passed without the repair:** The clock hasn't started. It runs from the day your notice reaches the landlord.
4. **You haven't given up the right by paying rent:** Met. You've paid no rent since the AC stopped. Paying rent while you know of the problem could waive this right (section 83.56(5)(a)). Whether a still-unfixed problem counts as a new "continuing noncompliance" isn't settled.

If you leave without meeting these steps, the landlord could claim you broke the lease. How much you could owe is outside this tool.

### Can you stop paying rent?
- Holding back rent risks an eviction case.
- The statutory defense is in section 83.60(1)(b). It applies to "a material noncompliance with s. 83.51 (1)". That covers codes, structure, and plumbing. It does not cover an item only your lease promises. Unless a local code covers AC, withholding rent over the AC isn't protected.
- If you did hold back rent and were sued, you would have to pay the rent into the court registry, or file a motion about the amount, within the short deadline stated in the summons. Missing it gives up your defenses (section 83.60(2)).
- The defense also requires a written notice that says you won't pay rent because of the problem. Your portal request didn't say that.

### What else can you do?
- **Damages:** Section 83.55 lets you recover damages caused by the landlord's failure to follow the lease. Amounts and court steps are outside this tool. A lawsuit can also make the loser pay the winner's attorney fees (section 83.48).
- **Code office:** A complaint to the code office is protected from retaliation (section 83.64), if you act in good faith.
- **If the landlord is trying but can't fix it:** Section 83.56(1) says that when the cause is beyond the landlord's control and the landlord keeps making every reasonable effort, the lease may be "terminated or altered by the parties." If you stay, rent for that period is reduced in proportion to the loss of rental value. If the home is untenantable and you leave, you owe no rent while it stays that way. The part being on order may bear on this. I'd need to know what the landlord has actually said about when the part arrives.

### Can you stop paying rent until the AC is fixed?
- Florida lets a tenant raise a landlord's failure to repair as a defense to an eviction for unpaid rent. It covers only failures to meet the duties in section 83.51(1), and section 83.60(1)(b) is the rule that says so.
- Those duties are building, housing and health codes, and, where no code applies, the structure and plumbing. Air conditioning isn't named in them.

### Can you break your lease?
Section 83.56(1) lets a tenant end the lease if the landlord "materially fails to comply with s. 83.51 (1) or material provisions of the rental agreement" within 7 days after getting a written notice. Here is how that applies to you.
- **A promise the landlord failed to keep:** Lease section 11 promises working AC, and it hasn't worked since June 3. This is met.
- **Whether the failure is "material":** The statute doesn't define the word, so this is not settled. One reading is that any failure to keep a lease promise is material. - **The notice:** Not met yet. Section 83.56(1) requires a written notice that names the problem and says you intend to end the lease because of it. Your June 4 portal request asked for a repair and didn't say that.

### Did you give the landlord the notice the law requires when leaving early?
Yes. You left before the lease's July 31, 2026 end date. This is the open point. - **Move-out date.** The notice to tenants says the landlord must give notice "WITHIN 30 DAYS AFTER YOU MOVE OUT" (83.49(2)(d)). Counting from April 15, the 30 days ended 2026-05-15, which has passed. On this reading the landlord lost any claim and must return the full $1,050.
- **Lease end date.** The rule begins "Upon the vacating of the premises for termination of the rental agreement," and it speaks of 30 days "after the termination of the rental agreement" (83.49(3)(a)). ### Does the law ban this kind of rent increase?

DETAILS

### Did you give the notice the law requires for leaving early?
Yes, on the facts you confirmed. You left before the lease's July 31, 2026 end. A tenant who does that must give "at least 7 days' written notice by certified mail or personal delivery to the landlord before vacating," and the notice "must include the address where the tenant may be reached" (83.49(5)). You handed your April 2 letter to the office, and it gave your new address. The last day to give notice for an April 15 move-out was April 8, so you were on time. Lease §7 also calls for hand delivery to the office, and you did that. The lease sets no different rule for leaving early.

### Was the landlord sent a proper reason to repair or lose you?
Your March 24 letter was handed to the office, named the toilet and the leak, and said you would end the lease. The 7 days ended March 31, and that date has passed (83.56(1), (4)). The pipes are plumbing, which the landlord must keep in reasonable working condition (83.51(1)(b)). You say you didn't cause the damage (83.51(4)). Your March rent was paid before the problem began, so you didn't waive anything by paying it (83.56(5)(a)). Whether this failure was "material" is not settled, because the statute doesn't define the word. One reading is that any failure of a listed plumbing duty is material. The other reading turns on how serious it was. Your toilet was the only one in the unit, and the pipe was leaking. That is the kind of fact each side would argue about. The point matters because it affects whether you validly ended the lease. It does not change the landlord's duty to handle the deposit.

The rule is that a landlord who plans to make a claim must send written notice by certified mail to your last known mailing address within 30 days after the rental agreement ends (83.49(3)(a)). If the landlord doesn't, it "forfeits the right to impose a claim upon the security deposit." It then "may not seek a setoff against the deposit but may file an action for damages after returning the security deposit to the tenant" (83.49(3)(a)). You've received no notice by any means.

When the 30 days run out depends on when the agreement ended, and that is not settled.

Under the moving-out reading, the landlord also had until April 30 to return the deposit if it planned no claim. Missing that date forfeits nothing while the 30 days for a claim notice are still running (83.49(3)(a)).

Even if the landlord does forfeit, it can still sue you for damages after returning the deposit. For example, it could argue you owe rent for the rest of the lease. That would turn on whether you validly ended the lease, which is the "material" question above.

Only a claim notice sent by certified mail to the address you gave counts as the required kind. If one arrives, you'd have 15 days after receiving it to object in writing (83.49(3)(b)). If you miss that deadline, you can still sue later (83.49(3)(b)).

If either side sues over the deposit, the winner gets court costs and a reasonable attorney fee, and the court moves the case up on its calendar (83.49(3)(c)).

- **Seven days:** The 7 days run from the day the notice reaches your landlord. No notice has been delivered, so the period hasn't started.
- **Rent paid with knowledge:** You paid May rent on May 1 knowing the garage was closed. Under 83.56(5)(a), paying rent with knowledge of a failure "waives his or her right to terminate the rental agreement or to bring a civil action for that noncompliance, but not for any subsequent or continuing noncompliance." The law doesn't settle how this applies here.
  - **One reading:** A garage that is still closed is a "continuing noncompliance," so paying rent gave up nothing.
  - **Other reading:** Paying with knowledge gave up your rights over this closure, and only a new failure would start over.

### Does the law reduce rent when a landlord can't provide something?
Only in one situation. Under 83.56(1)(b), rent is reduced in proportion to the loss when the failure is "due to causes beyond the landlord's control" and the landlord keeps making every reasonable effort to fix it. Here your landlord ordered the repaving. The office also gave you no reopening date. Those facts don't point to a cause beyond the landlord's control, though a court would decide that. If your landlord shows it is working to reopen the garage and the closure is beyond its control, you could raise this point.

### Are you protected if you complain?
Under 83.64(1), a landlord can't raise your rent, cut your services, or bring an action primarily to retaliate against you for a protected act. A written notice to end the lease under 83.56(1) is one of those acts. The law covers you only if you act in good faith, and a court decides what the landlord's reason was.
